nodes.title: Observed histories
nodes.summary: A prediction depends on which parts of a trajectory we choose to observe.

nodes.title: History improves Rule 110 prediction
nodes.summary: Short histories sharply reduce prediction error for the tested coarse observations of Rule 110.

nodes.title: History repair depends on the observation
nodes.summary: Rule 30 repairs strongly under derivative observation while its tested parity histories do not improve prediction.

nodes.title: Does strong history repair identify Class IV?
nodes.summary: The simple repair-only shortcut fails on the tested comparison rules.

nodes.title: What part of Rule 110 becomes predictable?
nodes.summary: History improves all three operational regions. Which gliders or interactions explain the remaining errors is still open.

nodes.title: Ether phase may explain much of the repair
nodes.summary: Phase recovery remains a plausible partial mechanism; measured history gains also extend to departure neighborhoods.

nodes.title: Separate background and disturbance errors
nodes.summary: A frozen regional comparison finds gains around departures and background across two detectors, two widths, and five observations.

nodes.title: Affine evolution has a constant commutator
nodes.summary: For binary affine evolution, the self-commutator equals the fixed bias.

nodes.title: Does a constant commutator imply affine evolution?
nodes.summary: The converse of the affine implication is false, already among elementary rules.

nodes.title: Nonlinear Rules 4 and 200 have zero commutator
nodes.summary: Exhaustive five-cell enumeration gives zero for every local commutator window of Rules 4 and 200.

nodes.title: Zero commutator is not a linearity test
nodes.summary: Observing an identically zero commutator does not establish that a rule is linear or affine.

nodes.title: History improves prediction around ether departures
nodes.summary: History reduces departure-region error in every tested seed comparison; those regions still contain most residual errors.

nodes.title: History beats the tested wider-snapshot estimator
nodes.summary: The 21-bit history beats the 21-bit snapshot at this training budget, while also having better context coverage.

nodes.title: Historical influence in the dynamics
nodes.summary: Past differences influence behavior when retained in the evolving state; this differs from giving an observer more history.

nodes.title: Controlled future repertoire
nodes.summary: Reachable outcomes under declared actions, observations, and a finite budget; a count does not specify the outcomes or how to reach them.

nodes.title: How does operation order change future options?
nodes.summary: Finite counterexamples separate option counts, outcome sets, and action responses; endogenous capabilities and viability remain open.

nodes.title: Enumerate continuations after both operation orders
nodes.summary: All states on 6-, 9-, and 11-cell rings were enumerated for 66 pairs, seven horizons, and two observations.

nodes.title: Outcome counts, sets, and action maps can differ separately
nodes.summary: Replayed finite examples show equal counts with different outcomes and equal outcome sets with different action responses.

nodes.title: When should an inherited primitive remain revisable?
nodes.summary: Costed one-transition and returning-task comparisons identify price-dependent revision benefits and policy failures; learning and changing the operation vocabulary remain open.

nodes.title: Compare fixed and revisable compiled primitives
nodes.summary: A bounded comparison prices compilation, physical execution, dispatch, retained traces, and revision; a causal-window follow-up removes finite-size coincidences.

nodes.title: What becomes possible when an organization dissolves?
nodes.summary: Distinguish loss of a unit, continued activity of its substrate, and formation of a new organization.

nodes.title: Wet alignment as an ongoing relationship
nodes.summary: An ethical motivation to preserve the capacity to learn and revise a relationship as interaction changes its participants.

nodes.title: Compiled primitives and their resource costs
nodes.summary: A macro reuses existing operations; its physical execution, dispatch, construction, and retained structure have distinct costs.

nodes.title: Expanding a macro preserves its physical computation
nodes.summary: With primitive operations still available and full expansion charged, adding macros does not enlarge physical-budget reachability.

nodes.title: A retained trace can pay for a nearby change
nodes.summary: At the declared prices, all-width programs give a narrow revision advantage for most one-letter changes; distant changes usually favor replacement.

nodes.title: Finite-ring program equivalence need not generalize
nodes.summary: Two selected Rule 4/30 shortcuts agree on six cells but fail on 11,264 of the 131,072 unrestricted causal windows.

nodes.title: Audit compiled programs on every causal window
nodes.summary: The 17-cell window exhaustively checks all local inputs for programs up to eight ticks and repeats the cost model using all-width equivalence.

nodes.title: Compare returning tasks and revision policies
nodes.summary: An exact sequence comparison separates full-hindsight planning from reactive policies and tests whether repeated changes repay an editable trace.

nodes.title: A locally cheaper revision can cost more after a return
nodes.summary: A free-trace example saves one unit on the changed job but adds two when the old task returns; available revision does not guarantee good sequential decisions.

nodes.title: Equal immediate costs can conceal different future costs
nodes.summary: Two declared tie rules choose equally cheap current actions but incur different costs on a returning task.

nodes.title: Repeated changes can repay a retained construction record
nodes.summary: The fixed trace reserve can be amortized across repeated management opportunities under the same declared price schedule.

nodes.title: A shared space for states and rules
nodes.summary: An eight-bit pattern can act as configuration, rule table, or difference once a decoder is specified.

nodes.title: Eight neighbors can supply their center’s rule
nodes.summary: For either declared address axis, all 40,320 assignments give nine-essential-input, degree-four rules; 36,000 functions are distinct.

nodes.title: The state-to-rule assignment changes the dynamics
nodes.summary: Changing only the encoding or address axis changes finite dynamics; a consistent rotation of the whole construction preserves them.

nodes.title: Shared-space and spatial-selector enumeration
nodes.summary: The frozen protocol covers 168 complete finite graphs and 80,640 local assignment/axis cases.

nodes.title: Outer-totalistic dimensional encoding
nodes.summary: A rule with 2·3^d bits fits in the two adjacent layers of a (d+1)-dimensional neighborhood.

nodes.title: The dimensional interpreter respects complement and reflection
nodes.summary: For every positive dimension, complementing all bits and reflecting all coordinates commutes with the ternary interpreter.

nodes.title: States and their changes transform differently
nodes.summary: States transform by complement plus reflection; XOR changes transform by reflection alone, creating an explicit commutator covariance defect.

nodes.title: Which families remain compatible across dimensions?
nodes.summary: Exact column and block encodings now include Rule 90 inside the 2D interpreter; compatibility through further dimensions remains open.

nodes.title: Does dimensional persistence distinguish Class IV?
nodes.summary: The proposed association is untested; a broader lift is needed to include Rules 30, 106, and 110.

nodes.title: Spacetime content and generating provenance
nodes.summary: A panel has one content identity and can have multiple generating-rule derivations.

nodes.title: Rule ambiguity can exceed future ambiguity
nodes.summary: Several rules may fit a panel while agreeing on its requested natural continuation.

nodes.title: An action can expose hidden provenance differences
nodes.summary: Compatible generators may agree along the observed path and differ after the same intervention.

nodes.title: Exact spacetime provenance experiment
nodes.summary: All 256 rules and all initial states on widths 6/8/10 were checked across seven observation lengths and four future horizons.

nodes.title: Two elementary updates survive the column encoding test
nodes.summary: The all-height graph selects Rules 23/232 at cadence one; other returning codes can require wider neighborhoods.

nodes.title: Separated data planes form a dimensional conveyor
nodes.summary: A local proof gives data-preserving diagonal transport inside the same interpreter construction in every positive lower dimension.

nodes.title: Restoring a valid encoding need not restore its content
nodes.summary: Some damaged trajectories regain valid code with different logical content in the bounded two-row experiment.

nodes.title: Exact column compatibility experiment
nodes.summary: A frozen search and independent graph audit establish invariant families, with separate finite action and damage checks.

nodes.title: Six-cell blocks implement Rule 90 exactly
nodes.summary: A fixed 2D law combines logical neighbors by XOR under a six-cell encoding and two-tick sampling.

nodes.title: One physical process has several exact effective laws
nodes.summary: The same encoding and trajectory implement Rules 60, 102, and 90 under fixed changes of frame and cadence.

nodes.title: The bounded block and moving-frame test is complete
nodes.summary: An independent audit agrees on all 781,050 candidate outcomes, admitting 22 elementary targets within the frozen budget.

nodes.title: Does three-dimensional space support a distinctive representation?
nodes.summary: Proposed and currently parked: parallel work suggests a representation specific to three dimensions; its precise claim remains unspecified.

nodes.title: A logical action can depend on physical coordination
nodes.summary: A repeated two-cell flip has one logical response while its components and its isolated version depend strongly on context.

nodes.title: The tested Rule-90 defects do not recover within four ticks
nodes.summary: No initially invalid mask/background case returns at sampled ticks two or four, under the declared periodic and isolated interventions.

nodes.title: The finite-cone defect experiment is complete
nodes.summary: Independent implementations agree on 196,608 response fields and the complete recovery and pair-interaction records.
